chapter_summary.overview: Transactions simplify partial failures and concurrency by grouping reads and writes into a logical unit that either commits or aborts. The chapter unpacks ACID, distinguishes read committed, snapshot isolation, and serializable isolation, then analyzes dirty reads, dirty writes, read skew, lost updates, write skew, and phantoms. It explains MVCC, explicit locks, compare-and-set, and automatic lost-update detection. Finally it compares the three major ways of implementing serializable isolation: actual serial execution, two-phase locking (2PL), and serializable snapshot isolation (SSI).
major_sections: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction

Explain why multi-object transactions are useful.

Define dirty reads and dirty writes.
Explain read committed and its implementation.
Define read skew/nonrepeatable reads.

transactions.definition: Logical group of reads and writes treated as one unit.
transactions.abort: The transaction fails and database writes are discarded/undone.
transactions.benefit: Converts many partial-failure and concurrency cases into abort-and-retry.

acid.atomicity: Abortability when a transaction partially fails; not a concurrency property.
acid.consistency: Application-defined invariants remain valid; the application bears primary responsibility.
acid.isolation: Concurrent transactions should behave as though they do not interfere; strongest form is serializability.
acid.warning: 'ACID compliant' is not a precise statement of identical guarantees across products.

durability_details.single_node: Nonvolatile storage plus WAL or similar recovery log.
durability_details.replicated: May wait for replication to some number of nodes before acknowledging commit.

multi_object_transactions.isolation: Other transactions see either all or none of the grouped writes.

items: Commit may have succeeded even if acknowledgement was lost.
Retry under overload can worsen overload.
Permanent errors such as constraint violations should not be retried.
External side effects may occur even if the DB transaction aborts.
Client process can fail during retries.

read_committed.write_implementation: Object/row write lock held until commit or abort.
read_committed.read_implementation: Readers commonly see the previous committed value until the writer commits.

snapshot_isolation.definition: Each transaction reads from a consistent point-in-time snapshot.
snapshot_isolation.principle: Readers never block writers and writers never block readers.
snapshot_isolation.implementation: MVCC keeps multiple committed object versions.

mvcc.created_by: Transaction that created a row version.
mvcc.deleted_by: Transaction that marked a row version deleted.
mvcc.update: Delete old version + create new version.
visibility: Ignore writes from transactions in progress when the reader started.
Ignore writes from transactions started after the reader.
Other valid committed versions are visible.
mvcc.garbage_collection: Remove versions once no active transaction can see them.

lost_updates.definition: Concurrent read-modify-write cycles cause one change to clobber another.
lost_updates.cas_warning: Verify the database's semantics; a stale snapshot predicate can make CAS unsafe.

replicated_lost_updates.problem: Locks/CAS assume one up-to-date copy and do not directly fit multi-leader/leaderless replication.
replicated_lost_updates.approach: Keep concurrent siblings and merge later; commutative operations are especially useful.
replicated_lost_updates.warning: LWW is prone to lost updates.

write_skew.definition: Transactions read overlapping state, make decisions, then update different objects so a shared invariant is violated.
write_skew.doctor_example: Both doctors see two on call and independently go off call, leaving zero.
write_skew.not_prevented_by: Snapshot isolation in the implementations discussed.
write_skew.fallback: Explicitly lock rows the transaction depends on if possible.

phantoms.definition: A write changes the set of rows matching another transaction's search condition.
phantoms.materializing_conflicts: Create concrete lockable rows for otherwise phantom conflicts; considered a last resort.

serializability.definition: Outcome equivalent to executing transactions one at a time in some serial order.

serial_execution.idea: One transaction at a time on one thread.
why_practical: Active data can often fit in memory
serial_execution.stored_procedure_reason: Avoid interactive application/database network waits by sending the entire transaction program in advance.
serial_execution.scaling: Partition data and run one serial thread per independent partition.
serial_execution.cross_partition_cost: Transactions spanning partitions require lock-step coordination and are much slower.

two_phase_locking.shared_lock: Multiple readers allowed unless an exclusive lock exists.
two_phase_locking.exclusive_lock: Required for writes; no other lock holder allowed.
two_phase_locking.upgrade: Shared lock may be upgraded to exclusive.
two_phase_locking.why_two_phase: Locks acquired during transaction, released at transaction end.
two_phase_locking.deadlock: Mutual waiting; DB aborts one transaction.

predicate_and_range_locks.predicate_lock: Covers all current and future objects matching a search predicate.
predicate_and_range_locks.index_range_lock: Lower-overhead approximation attached to an index entry/range; also called next-key locking.
predicate_and_range_locks.fallback: Whole-table lock if no suitable index exists.

ssi.additional_mechanism: Detect serialization conflicts and abort unsafe transactions.
ssi.outdated_premise: A transaction makes a decision from snapshot state that is no longer true at commit time.
detects: Reads of stale MVCC versions whose conflicting writes later commit
Writes that affect data/predicates another transaction previously read
ssi.tripwire: Read tracking notifies potential conflicts rather than blocking.
tradeoffs: Coarse tracking may cause unnecessary aborts
advantages: Readers/writers do not block each other
Not limited to one CPU core

scenario_questions.scenario: A transaction inserts an order and updates inventory, then crashes halfway.
scenario_questions.question: What property prevents a partial DB state?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Atomicity aborts and undoes the transaction's writes.

scenario_questions.scenario: A client times out waiting for commit acknowledgement and retries.
scenario_questions.question: What risk exists?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: The first commit may have succeeded, so retry can duplicate work without deduplication.

scenario_questions.scenario: A transaction fails because of a permanent unique constraint violation.
scenario_questions.question: Retry?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Usually no; permanent errors are not useful retry candidates.

scenario_questions.scenario: T1 writes x=3 but has not committed. T2 reads x=3.
scenario_questions.question: Name the anomaly.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Dirty read.

scenario_questions.scenario: T2 overwrites T1's uncommitted write.
scenario_questions.question: Name the anomaly.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Dirty write.

scenario_questions.scenario: A $100 transfer is observed as $400 + $500.
scenario_questions.question: Name the anomaly and solution.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Read skew/nonrepeatable read; snapshot isolation provides a consistent snapshot.

scenario_questions.scenario: A backup runs for hours while writes continue.
scenario_questions.question: Why use snapshot isolation?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: The backup sees one consistent point in time.

scenario_questions.scenario: Two clients read counter=42 and both write 43.
scenario_questions.question: What happened?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Lost update; use atomic value=value+1 when possible.

scenario_questions.scenario: Game logic is too complex for one atomic expression.
scenario_questions.question: How prevent lost update?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Lock the relevant rows with SELECT FOR UPDATE before validating/updating.

scenario_questions.scenario: CAS predicate is evaluated on an old snapshot.
scenario_questions.question: Why can this fail?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: The condition may appear true despite a concurrent write, allowing a lost update.

scenario_questions.scenario: Two doctors both see count=2 and each sets only their own row off-call.
scenario_questions.question: What anomaly?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Write skew.

scenario_questions.scenario: Two room-booking transactions both see zero conflicts and insert overlapping bookings.
scenario_questions.question: What is happening?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Phantom-related write skew; snapshot isolation is insufficient.

scenario_questions.scenario: A username is claimed concurrently by two transactions.
scenario_questions.question: Simple defense?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Unique constraint.

scenario_questions.scenario: A phantom query returns zero rows so FOR UPDATE locks nothing.
scenario_questions.question: Last-resort workaround?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Materialize the conflict with concrete lock rows.

scenario_questions.scenario: A single-thread serial DB uses interactive client/server statements.
scenario_questions.question: Why slow?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: The only transaction thread waits on network round trips.

scenario_questions.scenario: Eight partitions exist but most transactions span several partitions.
scenario_questions.question: Why won't serial execution scale linearly?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Cross-partition lock-step coordination dominates.

scenario_questions.scenario: T1 holds a shared lock and T2 requests exclusive on same row.
scenario_questions.question: What happens?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: T2 waits until T1 ends.

scenario_questions.scenario: T1 waits for a lock held by T2 while T2 waits for T1.
scenario_questions.question: What happens?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Deadlock; DB aborts one transaction.

scenario_questions.scenario: A booking query locks a room/time index range and another txn inserts overlap.
scenario_questions.question: What mechanism is this?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Index-range/next-key locking approximating a predicate lock.

scenario_questions.scenario: Under SSI, T1 reads old state while T2's write is uncommitted; T2 commits before T1.
scenario_questions.question: What can happen?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: T1 may abort because its premise became stale.

scenario_questions.scenario: T1 reads an index range; T2 later writes into it under SSI.
scenario_questions.question: Does T2 block?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: No. Read tracking is a tripwire; serializability is checked via conflict detection.

scenario_questions.scenario: An SSI workload has extreme contention and frequent aborts.
scenario_questions.question: What performance problem follows?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Retries add more work and can reduce throughput.

short_answer_questions.question: Why are transactions an abstraction?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: They let applications treat multiple reads/writes as one logical commit-or-abort unit and ignore many partial-failure/concurrency cases.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is ACID consistency unusual?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: It is primarily about application-defined invariants rather than a guarantee the database can define by itself.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is durability never absolute?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Disks, replicas, firmware, filesystems, power, and backups can all fail; multiple techniques only reduce risk.

short_answer_questions.question: Why are multi-object transactions useful?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Related records, denormalized data, and secondary indexes often require coordinated changes.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is retry logic subtle?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Ambiguous commits, overload, permanent errors, external side effects, and client failure complicate retry.

short_answer_questions.question: What does read committed prevent?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Dirty reads and dirty writes, but not read skew or all write races.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is snapshot isolation good for analytics?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Long reads observe a stable snapshot while writers continue.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain MVCC.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Keep multiple row versions tagged by transaction IDs; readers select versions visible to their snapshot; obsolete versions are GC'd later.

short_answer_questions.question: Compare lost-update defenses.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Atomic DB updates, explicit locks, automatic conflict detection, or compare-and-set; replicated systems may merge siblings.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is write skew subtle?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Transactions can update different rows while violating one cross-object invariant, so ordinary same-row conflict detection misses it.

short_answer_questions.question: What is a phantom?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: A write changes the result of another transaction's search predicate, potentially invalidating a decision.

short_answer_questions.question: Why does serializability simplify correctness?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Concurrent execution behaves like some serial order, preventing the race conditions discussed.

short_answer_questions.question: When is serial execution practical?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Small fast in-memory OLTP transactions submitted as stored procedures and mostly restricted to one partition.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain 2PL.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Reads take shared locks, writes exclusive locks, locks remain until transaction end, and deadlocks cause abort/retry.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is 2PL operationally painful?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Blocking reduces concurrency, queues build, slow transactions inflate tail latency, and deadlocks waste work.

short_answer_questions.question: What do predicate locks solve?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: They protect search conditions—including rows that do not yet exist—from phantom writes.

short_answer_questions.question: How is SSI different from 2PL?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: SSI optimistically runs on snapshots and detects/aborts unsafe executions instead of blocking potential conflicts up front.

short_answer_questions.question: What does SSI's outdated-premise logic detect?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Whether a transaction's reads were invalidated by writes that committed before it, or whether later writes affected its earlier reads.

short_answer_questions.question: What controls SSI performance?

interview_style_questions.question: What can go wrong with transaction retries?
How do you prevent lost updates?
When is actual serial execution viable?

common_confusions.confusion: Atomicity means no concurrent observer can see a half-finished operation.
common_confusions.correction: In ACID, atomicity is abortability; concurrency is isolation.

common_confusions.confusion: The C in ACID is fully a database guarantee.
common_confusions.correction: The application defines and must preserve most invariants.

common_confusions.confusion: Read committed is enough to avoid all concurrency bugs.
common_confusions.correction: It allows read skew, lost updates, and write skew.
Snapshot isolation can permit write skew and phantom-related races.

common_confusions.confusion: Lost update and write skew are identical.
common_confusions.correction: Lost update clobbers changes to the same object; write skew can update different objects while breaking a shared invariant.
It depends on whether the conditional predicate observes the current value rather than a stale snapshot.

common_confusions.confusion: SELECT FOR UPDATE can always lock against future inserts.
common_confusions.correction: If no row exists, no ordinary row lock exists; predicate/range locking is needed.
Two-phase locking and two-phase commit are completely different.
SSI is optimistic and detects conflicts while allowing transactions to proceed.

practice_problems.prompt: Writes A and B succeed, C fails, transaction aborts. What remains?
A=$500,B=$500; transfer $100 A->B. Reader sees A=$400 and B=$500. What total/anomaly?
Two clients read 10, each increments, both write 11. Correct result?
T12 starts before T13 updates 500->400. What may T12 continue seeing?
Two on-call doctors both see count=2 and both go off call. Final count?
Booking query returns no rows and two txns insert same slot. Why ordinary row locks fail?
practice_problems.solution: No existing row existed to lock; this is a phantom predicate conflict.

practice_problems.prompt: T1 has shared lock; T2 requests exclusive. What happens?
T1 waits for B held by T2; T2 waits for A held by T1. Resolution?
practice_problems.solution: DB detects deadlock and aborts one transaction.

practice_problems.prompt: T1 reads a predicate; T2 changes it and commits first. What may SSI do to T1?
practice_problems.solution: Abort T1 because its premise may be stale.

practice_problems.prompt: 8 independent partitions and all txns are single-partition. Benefit?
practice_problems.solution: Each partition can run its own serial transaction thread/core and scale throughput across cores.

must_memorize: Durability is risk reduction, never absolute.
Read committed prevents dirty reads and dirty writes.
Snapshot isolation prevents read skew by using a consistent snapshot.
MVCC keeps multiple versions and uses transaction visibility rules.
Lost update defenses: atomic operations, locks, detection, CAS.
Write skew updates different objects based on the same stale premise.
Phantoms change a predicate result and can cause write skew.
Serializable isolation prevents the chapter's race conditions.
Three serializable approaches: serial execution, 2PL, SSI.
Serial execution favors short, in-memory, stored-procedure, single-partition transactions.
2PL is pessimistic: shared/exclusive locks, blocking, deadlocks, range locks.
SSI is optimistic: snapshot reads plus serialization-conflict detection and aborts.
SSI performance is strongly affected by contention and abort rate.
final_review.memory_chain: TRANSACTION -> ACID -> RETRY -> READ COMMITTED -> DIRTY READ/WRITE -> READ SKEW -> SNAPSHOT/MVCC -> LOST UPDATE -> WRITE SKEW -> PHANTOM -> SERIALIZABLE -> SERIAL EXECUTION -> 2PL -> PREDICATE LOCKS -> SSI
final_review.one_sentence_takeaway: Weak isolation removes some race conditions while leaving others to application code; serializable execution aims to make concurrent transactions behave like a correct one-at-a-time history.
